newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee seen stable against dlr until March 97.
newsitem.headline: India rupee seen stable against dlr until March 97.

text.p: The Indian rupee is expected to weather the impact of large external payments of more than $5.0 billion before the end of March 1997 and hold largely steady against the dollar, bank dealers and analysts said on Tuesday.

"I don't see too much of a depreciation (of the rupee) till March," said Janak Desai, chief forex dealer at Standard Chartered Bank in Bombay. "The problem for the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) has been appreciation of the rupee all these months."

The country's central bank has been buying spot dollars in recent months, mainly to arrest the appreciation of the rupee fueled by a large supply of dollars from foreign direct investment and portfolio investment.
The rupee was trading at 35.88/90 per dollar in mid-morning trade on Tuesday.
"The RBI has been trying to match cash flows with debt repayment," said Desai. "I guess they want to meet their obligations without depleting reserves."
Substantial dollar inflows have also come through commercial loans raised by Indian companies in global markets.
A slowdown in Indian imports also has helped the rupee rise.
India's foreign currency assets were $19.39 billion on November 29, down from $19.53 billion on November 22 and up from $17.30 billion on December 1, 1995.

Bankers and economists said India has to repay close to $6.0 billion between December and March towards maturing India Development Bonds, FCNRA (foreign currency non-resident account deposits held by expatriate Indians) and IMF debt repayment.
India's financial year runs from April to March.
Last week, the RBI began rolling over its earlier forward dollar transactions maturing in December, totalling an estimated $700 million.
RBI has been gently nudging the rupee down by hiking its dollar buying price to 35.80 from 35.30 level earlier this year.
The rupee touched a historic low of 38.50 in a speculative frenzy in February, but recovered to the 34 level in March.
A sudden spurt in dollar demand, attributed mostly to the rising oil import bills incurred by state-run oil firms, pushed down the rupee to the 35.88/90 level on Monday.

"We are expecting the rupee to touch 36.50 to a dollar in the next six months," said the treasurer of a French bank in Bombay. He said the depreciation will be more or less in line with the inflation differentials.

"We expect the rupee to depreciate by about 2.5 percent from current levels by March 31, 1997," said Chetan Ahya, analyst at Caspian Research in Bombay, attributing it to pressures of debt repayment. Thereafter it will about 6.0 percent a year, he said.
"We are not worried about the rupee," he said.
Economists said the RBI would not want a sharp decline in the rupee until March as it would worsen the fiscal deficit, which the government is trying to contain at 5.0 percent of GDP.
Beyond March, the RBI would like the rupee to depreciate a little faster to sharpen India's export competitiveness, analysts said.
The 1997 budget and the inward flows through foreign investment in 1997 also would be critical factors determining the exchange rate, they said.

The independent Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) said the first seven months of 1996/97 (April-March) saw $1.83 billion in foreign fund investment on Indian bourses against $861 million in the year-ago period.
"Likewise, GDR (global depositary receipt) flotations (by Indian firms) were $916 million compared to $136 million (in the year-ago period," CMIE said in its November monthly review.
